question: Does published work contradict the current assessment: Three distinctions are claimed: (i) the temporal term is attached post hoc to an arbitrary base retriever, whereas the closest systems hard-code temporal handling in a fixed pipeline; (ii) it targets continuously amended statutes/regulations with near-duplicate successive versions and validity intervals, whereas existing temporal benchmarks are ESG disclosures, financial filings and date-annotated web QA, and existing regulatory retrieval work is static; (iii) it can express validity/as-of membership, whereas the published hybrids use recency decay. Each distinction is plausible but each is currently only an untested framing or an absent resource, not a demonstrated finding.?
description: Assessment: substantial_overlap. The problem framing and the temporal-decay mechanism are already published, and the benchmark/evaluation recipe is established in adjacent domains; the residual contribution exists but is currently framed as the part that is most pre-empted. Evidence is sufficient to judge overlap (two closest methods plus a full-text survey and a full-text temporal-decay system) but only abstract-level for the two closest papers, and the decisive experiment (cross-retriever, validity-aware, amended-statute benchmark) has not been run. Hence 'substantial_overlap' rather than 'weak_or_flawed' (the idea is coherent and testable) or 'promising_needs_validation' (the mechanism is not novel enough to warrant that label without reframing).
confidence_basis: Direct full-text evidence from a legal-retrieval review that names clause-granularity versioning as an unaddressed failure mode, states that diachronic failure is least integrated into mainstream practice, and asserts that solutions are stronger at representation than at retrieval-time enforcement; corroborated by earlier findings that the same source reports no empirical comparison.
rationale: The assessment was formed from work found around the initial idea; look for work that would invalidate it.
resolution: Resolved: the three distinctions should not be presented as independent novelty claims. (iii) validity/as-of semantics is conceptually pre-empted - legal retrieval already requires distinguishing valid time from transaction time and names point-in-time resolution a legality-critical operation. (ii) clause-granularity versioning is a recognized but explicitly unaddressed gap ('versioned only at document granularity, producing whole-document snapshots that obscure structural-unit differentials'), so the benchmark is valuable but identifying the gap is not novel. (i) retrieval-time enforcement is described as under-explored ('most solutions remain stronger at representation than at retrieval-time enforcement'), which rationalizes a post-hoc ranking layer but is still an untested framing until measured. Consequence: the contribution must be the implementation and measurement - valid-time gating enforced at retrieval time, evaluated across base retrievers with clause-level contamination and point-in-time recovery - not the identification of the problem or the naming of the signal.
